specPoints.text: understand how ions are formed by electron loss or gain

know the charges of these ions: • metals in Groups 1, 2 and 3 • non-metals in Groups 5, 6 and 7 • Ag+, Cu2+, Fe2+, Fe3+, Pb2+, Zn2+ • hydrogen (H+), hydroxide (OH–), ammonium (NH4+), carbonate (CO3 2–), nitrate (NO3-), sulfate (SO4 2–).

primer.text: Ions are already explained: electrons lost or gained to reach a full outer shell, metals losing for positive, non-metals gaining for negative. This note turns that idea into a memorised toolkit - which charges each group gives, and the compound ions that keep appearing in equations.

lessons.title: How to Deduce the Charge of an Ion
sourceHeadings: How to deduce the charge of an ion
lessons.opening: A group number plus one look at the outer shell settles most charges: count the outer electrons, then decide whether giving them away or topping up is easier. Fewer than four outer electrons points to donating and a positive ion; more than four points to receiving and a negative one.
keyPoints: Deducing a charge starts from the outer electron shell: count the electrons sitting there.
Atoms with fewer than four outer electrons donate them and form positive ions.
Atoms with more than four outer electrons receive electrons and form negative ions.
Group 1, 2 and 3 metals give 1+, 2+ and 3+ ions; group 5, 6 and 7 non-metals take 3-, 2- and 1-.
Compound ions are ions made from more than one element, and their formulae must be learned as given.

low.restatement: To deduce a charge, count the outer-shell electrons and ask which is easier: handing extras over or filling the gap. Under four means donate and go positive; over four means receive and go negative.
low.analogy: Think of hands of cards: a player holding only a couple of cards deals them away to leave the table, while a player with an almost-complete set picks up the one card that finishes it.
low.examPointer: Group numbers make this quick: group 2 means 2+, group 7 means 1- - the charge follows the group without any working.

medium.restatement: The method is count, then judge: outer-shell electrons first, then the donate-or-receive call, with four as the hinge. Group position shortcuts the whole judgement, which is why the group 1 to 3 and group 5 to 7 patterns are quoted directly.
medium.analogy: A nearly-empty coach with few passengers drops everyone off and travels light - the donor side. A coach one seat short of full keeps collecting passengers until it is complete - the receiving side.
medium.examPointer: Compound ions break the single-element habit: ammonium, hydroxide, carbonate, nitrate and sulfate arrive as ready-made chunks whose formulae and charges ride together.

check.stem: What is the first move when deducing the charge an atom will carry?

options.text: Count the electrons in the outer electron shell
options.explanation: The outer-shell count drives everything that follows; the method starts there.

options.text: Count all the electrons the atom holds
options.explanation: Total electrons describe the neutral atom; only the outer shell decides the charge.

options.text: Read the atomic number off the periodic table
options.explanation: Atomic numbers count protons; the charge comes from the outer electrons.

options.text: Memorise the charge with no method behind it
options.explanation: Memory helps, but the method backs it up when an unfamiliar ion appears.

check.stem: An atom has fewer than four outer electrons. What does it do, and what follows?

options.text: It donates the electrons and becomes a positive ion
options.explanation: Fewer than four means giving is easier, and giving leaves a positive charge.

options.text: It receives electrons and becomes a negative ion
options.explanation: Receiving suits atoms already past four; this atom sits below the hinge.

options.text: It shares electrons to fill the shell
options.explanation: Sharing belongs to covalent bonding; charge deduction here assumes transfer.

options.text: It does nothing, being already stable
options.explanation: A shell short of a full set is not complete, so the atom reacts.

check.stem: What charge does a group 2 metal ion carry?

options.explanation: Two outer electrons donated leaves the ion two units positive.
The negative sign belongs to receivers; group 2 metals donate.
That is group 1's charge; group 2 donates two electrons.
Three is the group 3 pattern; this row donates only two.

check.stem: What charge does a group 6 non-metal ion carry?

options.explanation: Six outer electrons means two short of a full shell, so two arrive and the charge is 2-.
Non-metals receive rather than donate, so the sign stays negative.
The group number is not the charge; only the gap to a full shell counts.
That is group 7's pattern; group 6 needs two electrons.

check.stem: What makes an ion a compound ion?

options.text: It is built from more than one element
options.explanation: Compound ions such as OH- and NH4+ carry several elements under one overall charge.

options.text: It carries a charge greater than 1
options.explanation: Charge size is unrelated; some single-element ions carry 2+ or 3-.

options.text: It forms only from transition metals
options.explanation: Compound ions are about joined elements, not about which block the metal sits in.

options.text: It is a molecule with no charge
options.explanation: Molecules are neutral; compound ions carry their charge like any other ion.

lessons.title: Common Positive and Negative Ions
sourceHeadings: Common ions with a positive charge
Common ions with a negative charge
lessons.opening: The exam expects a memorised table: groups 1 to 3 give their metal ions at 1+, 2+ and 3+, the named metals carry set charges such as Fe2+ and Fe3+, and the compound ions - hydroxide, ammonium, carbonate, nitrate, sulfate - ride their own fixed charges. Group 5, 6 and 7 non-metals take 3-, 2- and 1-.
keyPoints: Metals in groups 1, 2 and 3 form ions of 1+, 2+ and 3+ respectively.
Non-metals in groups 5, 6 and 7 form ions of 3-, 2- and 1- respectively.
Silver carries 1+, copper(II), lead(II) and zinc carry 2+, and iron appears as both 2+ and 3+.
Hydrogen rides as H+ alongside the metal ions.
The compound ions to know are hydroxide OH-, ammonium NH4+, carbonate CO3 2-, nitrate NO3- and sulfate SO4 2-.

low.restatement: Two tables carry this note: the positive side, where group metals and named metals sit with their set charges, and the negative side, where group non-metals and the compound ions do the same. All of it is recall material for the exam.
low.analogy: Treat the compound ions like pre-assembled tool kits: nobody rebuilds a hammer mid-job, they reach for it whole. NH4+ and SO4 2- arrive complete, charge included, ready to slot into any formula.
low.examPointer: The note's exam hint is blunt: every charge in both tables is assumed knowledge, so drill them until the recall is instant.

medium.restatement: The positive table splits into group patterns and named metals: Ag+ stands alone while copper, iron and lead carry their set charges under Roman numerals. The negative table pairs group charges with the five compound ions whose subscripts and charges must be written together.
medium.analogy: Named-metal charges work like surnames that never change: silver is always Ag+, just as a shop sign stays fixed. Compound ions work like postcodes - digits and letters travel as one bundle, never split.
medium.examPointer: Writing ionic formulae later leans on exactly these charges: the crossing-over method only works when NH4+, OH- and CO3 2- are recalled without hesitation.

check.stem: Which formula and charge belong to the silver ion?

options.explanation: Silver sits outside the group rules with its own fixed charge of 1+.
A 2+ pattern from nearby metals does not transfer to silver.
No table row gives silver a 3+; its charge is fixed at 1+.
Silver is a metal, and metals appear on the positive side only.

check.stem: Iron appears in the table twice. Which pair of charges does it carry?

options.explanation: Iron(II) is Fe2+ and iron(III) is Fe3+; both rows are assumed knowledge.
No row shows iron at 1+; the pair is 2+ with 3+.
Dropping the iron(III) row loses half the pair.
Negative signs belong to the non-metal and compound-ion side.

check.stem: What is the formula and charge of the zinc ion?

options.explanation: The table lists Zinc(II) at 2+, one fixed charge.
Zinc does not follow the group 1 pattern; it is a named metal at 2+.
That is the group 3 pattern, not zinc's.
Zinc sits on the positive side; the negative sign cannot apply.

check.stem: Which is the correct formula and charge for the nitrate ion?

options.explanation: Nitrate is the compound ion: one nitrogen with three oxygens, charge 1-.
That is the group 5 single-element pattern; nitrate is the compound ion, not a lone nitrogen.
That is the carbonate ion's label; nitrate carries one oxygen fewer and a single negative charge.
Nitrate is a negative ion; the table lists it at 1-.

check.stem: Which pair correctly matches compound ion to formula and charge?

options.explanation: Both rows come straight from the tables: ammonium positive at 1+, carbonate negative at 2-.
Both signs are backwards: ammonium is the positive one, carbonate the negative.
The ammonium subscript is 4, and carbonate's charge is 2-, not 1-.
Ammonium carries a single positive charge, and carbonate carries 2-, so both halves are wrong here.

glossary.definition: An ion built from more than one element, carrying one overall charge.
The outermost shell of electrons, whose count decides the charge an atom adopts.
The negative compound ion OH-, charge 1-.
The positive compound ion NH4+, charge 1+.
The negative compound ion CO3 2-, charge 2-.
The negative compound ion NO3-, charge 1-.
The negative compound ion SO4 2-, charge 2-.
